paras: The lynching of Sam and John Campbell took place about midnight on December 23-24, 1880, when a party of men took the two young Black brothers from the jail at Munfordville, Hart County, Kentucky, and hanged them from a tree. The brothers had been arrested that day, accused of beating and robbing John A. Gardner, a prominent Hart County citizen styled "Esquire," who lived about a mile from Rowlett's Station. The story ran within days in papers from Connecticut to Texas and Minnesota, usually under headlines naming the victims only as "negroes."

According to a Horse Cave special to the Louisville Courier-Journal, Sam Campbell lived with Gardner, and his brother John, from the neighborhood, had stayed there the night before. They were about 20 and 23 years old and had "only been in the country a few months"; John's people were said to live in Taylor County.

About daylight on Thursday, December 23, Sam Campbell called Gardner to his barn, telling him that one of his cows was sick. On entering, Gardner was struck on the head and face with "a large logwood stick" and robbed of about $130. The shorter wire report said Campbell then told Mrs. Gardner what had happened and helped carry her husband into the house, but that suspicion "nevertheless" fell on him and his brother.
The two were arrested, reportedly found with a pocketbook and money ($132.50 by one count) that Mrs. Gardner identified as her husband's, and jailed at Munfordville.

Around midnight a party the Courier-Journal put at "seventy-five or one hundred men" came to the jail and demanded the keys. The jailer, judging resistance useless, handed them over and asked only that the other prisoners not be disturbed, which the men promised. The brothers were led through the streets and down a hillside between the town and the river and hanged from the limb of a tree; one printing opened, "Side by side they hang on the banks of Green river."
The Courier-Journal wrote that "it is said" Sam confessed before he died and blamed John for persuading him, while John was "stubborn." Other versions said one brother, or both, confessed.

The coroner summoned a jury of six men, which held an inquest and returned a verdict "in accordance with the facts." Gardner was reported in very critical condition with several wounds to his face and head, and some papers expected his injuries to prove fatal. No member of the mob was named, and no report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry, or Gardner's later condition was found.

Most papers drew on two Kentucky dispatches of December 24: the long Courier-Journal special, carried by the Chicago Tribune and the Rock Island Argus, and a shorter Horse Cave telegram printed by the Richmond Dispatch, the Wheeling Intelligencer, the Dallas Herald and the Wheeling Register. A separate Cincinnati Star special from Munfordsville appeared in the Omaha Bee, and a two-sentence Louisville item ran in the St. Paul Daily Globe and was reprinted by Minnesota weeklies. Weekly news digests in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Mississippi, Arkansas and South Carolina carried condensed versions into January 1881.

Several headlines treated the hanging as deserved punishment: the Morning Journal and Courier ran it as "Swift Retribution for Murderers," although Gardner was still alive, and the Chicago Tribune called the brothers "Two Murderous and Thieving Negroes." Others framed it as Kentucky custom, as in the Wheeling Intelligencer's "The Usual Kentucky Tragedy" and the Indiana State Sentinel's "How They Serve 'Em in Kentucky." Plainer heads such as "Negro Robbers Hanged by a Mob" (Dallas) and "Wicked Work" (St. Paul) still stated the brothers' guilt as fact: "two negroes nearly killed and robbed" Gardner.

Reports of the mob's size ranged from 75 to "about one hundred," and only the Cheyenne Leader said the men were masked. The Omaha Bee's Star special said the brothers were taken from "the jail at Roulletteville station," while the Courier-Journal and the wire placed the jail at Munfordville and described the route from that town to the river. The Cheyenne Leader reversed the brothers' roles, making John the boy who lived with Gardner, and one weekly named the victim of the robbery "Joseph Gardner."

reader.title: Lynching of Sam and John Campbell
bases: A party of 75 to 100 men took two Black brothers held on a robbery charge from the Munfordville jail and hanged them from a tree (A1, A2, A3).

Sam and John Campbell were taken from jail without any legal proceeding and hanged by a party reported at 75 to 100 men (A1, A2, A4), in punishment for the robbery and beating of John A. Gardner of which they were accused (A1, A21).

Three separately sourced dispatches, the Courier-Journal's Horse Cave special (A1), the short Horse Cave wire (A2, A5) and a Cincinnati Star special from Munfordsville (A9), agree that the two Campbell brothers were taken from jail by a mob and hanged.

accounts.label: Courier-Journal Horse Cave special (Louisville, Dec. 24)
accounts.gist: Full narrative: Sam lived with Gardner and lured him to the barn; the brothers were found with Gardner's pocketbook, jailed at Munfordville, and taken at midnight by 75 or 100 men who got the keys from the jailer and hanged them on a hillside toward the river; Sam is said to have confessed.

accounts.label: Short Horse Cave wire (Dec. 24)
accounts.gist: Campbell called Gardner to the stable, where he was knocked down with a stick and robbed of $130; Campbell then helped carry him in, but $132 was found on the brothers, and 100 men took them from the Munfordsville jail at midnight and hanged them; one confessed.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Star special from Munfordsville
accounts.gist: Two Campbell brothers, colored, arrested for robbery and attempted murder of Squire J. A. Gardner, were taken by a mob from the jail at 'Roulletteville station' and hanged.

accounts.label: Louisville brief
accounts.gist: Two negroes nearly killed and robbed Gardner at 'Romletts station' and were taken from jail by 75 men (or 100 masked men) and hanged.

framing.detail: The Morning Journal and Courier headed the story 'Swift Retribution for Murderers' though Gardner was alive; the Chicago Tribune called the brothers 'Two Murderous and Thieving Negroes'.
Northern papers framed it as Kentucky custom: 'The Usual Kentucky Tragedy' (Wheeling Intelligencer), 'How They Serve 'Em in Kentucky' (Indiana State Sentinel).
Most papers ran the wire or the Louisville brief under plain heads ('Lynched', 'Two Negroes Lynched in Kentucky', 'Negro Robbers Hanged by a Mob'), stating the brothers' guilt as fact.

conflicts.note: Only the Cheyenne Leader brief mentions masks.
The Courier-Journal special and the wire both name Munfordville and describe the route from the town to the river; the Star special's brief line is likely a conflation with the robbery site.
